text: Two tyres. The same nail. One goes flat in seconds. The other keeps rolling for miles. So what's hiding inside?
Open up an old style tyre, and you find a second one inside. A soft rubber doughnut, called the inner tube.
The air goes into the tube, not the tyre. The tube swells up like a balloon, and pushes the tyre out against the road.
The tough outer tyre is just armour. On its own, it can't hold any air.
Now the tubeless tyre. Open it up, and... nothing. No tube at all!
Instead, the inside of the tyre is lined with a thin airtight skin. And its edges sit tight against the metal rim.
Pump in air, and the pressure itself shoves those edges onto the rim. The harder it pushes, the tighter it seals.
Here comes the nail. In the tube tyre, it pops the balloon. The air rushes out around the tube, and escapes through the wheel. Flat, in seconds.
In the tubeless tyre, the thick rubber squeezes around the nail and grips it. The air only leaks slowly. You can often drive on to a garage.
And the repair? A tube tyre has to come off the wheel. A tubeless one gets a rubber plug, pushed in from outside. Minutes.
There's more. A tube rubs against the tyre and makes heat. No tube means less heat, and less weight.
So why do tubes still exist? Wire spoke wheels are full of holes, so most of them need one. And a tube is cheap to replace.
The winner for everyday roads? Tubeless. Because it fails slowly. And slow is safe.

It pops up on the other screen in about a second. And thirty minutes later, it's gone.
Orbi Transfer dot com. Same nail. Very different ending.
